submission.natural_language_explanation: Retrospective detector of the vocabulary of abstract construal - the words a written text uses to frame, ask about, classify and organize its subject rather than to name concrete things and physical events. It peaks (0.9-1.6) on (i) the interrogative words what, why and how (and less reliably whether, where, when, which) opening a question or an embedded question ('she explained how...' 1.20, 'we know what you mean' 1.0-1.3, 'it is uncertain whether...' 0.77); (ii) the links of, for, about and on when they carry the complement of an abstract head ('a common method of raising money' 1.56, 'several reasons for the delay' 1.54, 'types of soil' 1.0, 'tips for saving money' 0.94, 'the criteria for the award' 0.69, 'an overview of' 0.84) but only weakly (0-0.3) when the same links attach to a concrete, partitive, temporal or proper head ('a loaf of bread' 0.0, 'ten minutes for the bus' 0.2-0.3, 'for three hours' 0.0, 'the College of' 0.0); (iii) the verbs of describing, explaining, analysing and organizing (describe, explain, discuss, suggest, recommend, consider, examine, compare, present) at 0.6-1.5, with the abstract head nouns they take (aspect, method, reasons, criteria, overview, type, framework, view, information, research, quality) firing more weakly and unevenly on their own (0.2-0.95: overview and aspect strongest, method and results weakest) and clearly when a link or an exposition verb sits beside them; and (iv) the connectives and quantifiers of written argument (although, while, because, however, moreover, thus, therefore, still, even, only, such, both, each, several, most, all, another, indeed) at 0.5-1.2, and 'and'/'or' where it coordinates abstract words ('research and', 'quality and', 'cultural and' 0.6-0.9) but not concrete or human ones ('children and', 'men and' 0.0). It stays in the 0-0.4 band on narration and physical procedure - personal pronouns, the definite article, concrete nouns for objects, substances, places and people (roof, tiles, rope, bread, oven, soil, ice), physical verbs (leaked, carried, poured, hammered, washed, sat) and measurements - and because a text's first token is read with no context whatever, its first-position value is a bare-token prior (high on A/An, numerals, what/why/how/whether/when, although, this, about; near zero on he/she/they/my, the, in/at), so predictions of inactivity are for the text from its second token onward.

rival_explanations: Narrower, frame-only reading: the pole detects complement frames rather than a register, so besides the interrogatives it should fire on of/for/about only where an abstract head actually governs a complement, and any abstract noun or exposition verb standing without a complement (the system, the process, describe it again) should stay inactive.

Broader, plain abstractness reading: the pole is a general abstract-versus-concrete register detector, so it should also fire on abstract nouns and nominalizations that take no complement (the conclusion, the problem, the process) and on any abstract word embedded in otherwise concrete narration.

Structural reading: the pole marks document layout rather than construal - headings, colons, newlines, list markers and section words (Overview, Steps, Results, Table of Contents, 'A.', Reference:) - so it should fire on section headings and list cues of any content and fall away in running body prose.

Artificial satellites are first launched into the desired altitude by conventional liquid/solid propelled rockets after which the satellite may use onboard propulsion systems for orbital stationkeeping. Once in the desired orbit, they often need some form of attitude control so that they are correctly pointed with respect to the Earth, the Sun, and possibly some astronomical object of interest. They are also subject to drag from the thin atmosphere, so that to stay in orbit for a long period of time some form of propulsion is occasionally necessary to make small corrections (orbital station-keeping). Many satellites need to be moved from one orbit to another from time to time, and this also requires propulsion. A satellite’s useful life is usually over once it has exhausted its ability to adjust its orbit.

Here, where our Sun is so far away that it hangs suspended in an alien sky of perpetual twilight, looking just like a particularly large star traveling through a sea of smaller stars, is the Kuiper Belt--a mysterious, distant deep-freeze that astronomers are only now first beginning to explore. Makemake is a denizen of this remote region, a dwarf planet that is one of the largest known objects inhabiting the Kuiper Belt, sporting a diameter that is about two-thirds the size of Pluto. In April 2016, a team of astronomers announced that, while peering into the outer limits of our Solar System, NASA's Hubble Space Telescope (HST) discovered a tiny, dark moon orbiting Makemake, which is the second brightest icy dwarf planet--after Pluto--in the Kuiper Belt.

The Pendulum Ball Exercise
This is an excellent exercise for visual tracking and convergence work. A pendulum ball is simply a ball tied on a string and hanging down from the ceiling or light fixture. The ball can travel side to side like a pendulum does, it can travel in a circle (clockwise or counter clockwise) and it can move in and out towards the participant's face. When traveling in and out, it is a convergence exercise and can be used before or after the Brock String Exercise. Visual tracking is important for reading and writing and convergence is important for copying information from a board.
Pendulum balls can be purchased or made. One way to make them is to obtain a solid ball, drill a hole through it with a drill and thread a string through it a little less than the diameter of the hole and tie a couple of knots at the end. We like putting numbers and letters on the ball so the participants can have something to focus on as the ball travels. Stickers or stamps of animals or other designs can be used for younger children.
When doing this exercise, it is important for the participant to keep their head still and only move their eyes to track the pendulum ball.
Step by Step Instructions: The Pendulum Ball Exercise.
1. Obtain or make a Pendulum ball. Attach it to something high so that the ball rests at eye level. There should be plenty of room for the ball to swing in any direction without hitting anything, including the participant.
2. The simplest exercise is to push the ball so that it swings from side to side like a pendulum. Have the participant watch the ball, trying to see if she/he can read some of the letters or numbers on the ball. Make sure they follow the ball with their eyes and not with their head. Their head should be still. At first some participants may need to have their head held still until they get used to not moving their head and only move their eyes. For beginners and those with limited tracking skills, quit the exercise after about 5 minutes.
3. When step two is mastered (i.e., the participant can watch a pendulum ball and track for about 4 minutes without losing focus or sight of the ball) or close to mastery, then move the pendulum ball in a counter clock wise direction so that it is moving in a circle going close to the participant's nose (at 6:00) and then away from their nose (at 12:00 on an horizontal imaginary clock). The participant is to do this for two minutes.
4. After the two minutes, the participant is to track the pendulum ball going in a clock wise direction.
5. After the two minutes of tracking the pendulum ball in a clock wise direction, the participant is to track the ball being swung in a direction towards their nose. This is to be done not in a circle but swinging back and forth. The participant is to track the ball for 60 seconds to two minutes.
6. After five to six minutes, the session is over.

Before knowing what infrastructure engineering is, it is very important to understand the basic meaning of the word infrastructure. The term infrastructure refers to the collection of virtual and physical resources supporting the entire IT background.
The engineers, architects, designers and the planners use this term to describe various facilities, organizational structures, facilities and services for the residential community, apartment building, city or even a nation.
What is Infrastructure engineering?
Infrastructure Engineering is literally a branch of engineering, which organizes all the systems for a particular engineering project. It takes the charge of coordinating the entire project whether it is simple, complex or a very big structure.
In modern times, we consider infrastructure as any facility or service, but it’s not that simple. Infra means below or the underground, like gas supply or water supply system which is not visible. So, it takes into account all these tasks and projects.
• Mass Transit Systems
• Roads and Bridges
• Highways and Railway Transportation
• Water and Sewage Systems
• Power and gas grids
• Waterways, ports, and canals
• Law management and prisons
• Electrical power and connections
• Fire stations and equipment
• Importance of Infrastructure Engineering
Importance of Infrastructure Engineering
This trade includes the management of infrastructure supporting human activities, designing, analysis of various systems like water and wastewater management, oil and gas, electric power, communication, transportation services and the buildings making urban and rural environment. These civil engineers deliver indispensable services like providing shelter, economic development, and social interactions. In simple words, it deals with all those things which are the lifeline for every individual.
The essential factor that infrastructure engineers focus on is working on the projects for the whole community rather than targeting any individual. They pay attention to how different systems will work together in the community and fulfill their needs.
Every individual use these infrastructure systems, and also wish that it shall work properly, but the point is they do not like paying for it. There is a need to understand their importance. Making it work randomly may lead to a lot of loss. Hence, it is important to understand the need of this infrastructure commerce to make things work in an exact manner.
To elaborate: Public utilities and transportation systems are important for the economic stability as well as the growth of the community and the businesses. Similarly, the safety of the residents, employees, the accumulation of the fuel and other natural resources, access to clean water and sanitary disposals, etc. are looked by the infrastructure engineers who help solve many problems and avoid any loss.

Only a decade ago, the image below could only have been the stuff of Hollywood fiction—if that. Two black males conversing in the White House: One is the President, the other a modern-day tinkerer who may well be on his way to becoming a world-class engineer.
Another surreal detail: The President is holding the tinkerer’s 3D-printed replica of the same edifice they’re standing in. (In the featured image above, he is blowing bubbles through a wand 3D-printed from the same tinkerer’s collection.)
For practically his entire life, 9-year-old Jacob Leggette, a resident of Baltimore, Maryland, has seen a black man in the White House. A participant in the 2016 White House Science Fair, held on 13 April, Leggette’s specialty is experimenting with 3D printers and other types of digital manufacturing technologies. His next goal is to experiment with the 3D printing of artificial organs, which is actually a thing.
It’s that kind of bold thinking that may someday result in a black Nobel-prize-winning scientist.
That pioneer could be one of these young scholars (participants in a previous White House Science Fair):
“As a society, we have to celebrate outstanding work by young people in science at least as much as we do Super Bowl winners,” said President Barack Obama about the White House Science Fair, an event he started in 2010. “Because superstar biologists and engineers and rocket scientists and robot-builders…They’re the folks who are going to come up with cures for diseases and new sources of energy, and help us build healthier, more successful societies.”
Since its inception, the White House Science Fair has invited hundreds of young aspiring scientists and engineers to showcase their ideas and handiwork to the President, and ultimately the world. Of the 39 projects presented this year, six of them (including Leggette’s) were led by a young black boy or girl.

So, for their Lemelson-MIT InvenTeam invention, they built a 100-lb robot that moves along subway system rails, vacuuming up debris to make New York City’s transportation system cleaner and more efficient for kids like them who take the subway to school every day.

'The ancient region of Kamarupa finds no mention in the Ashokan records (3rd Century B.C.).[60m] The first dated mention comes from the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st Century), which describes a people called Sêsatai. The second mention comes from Ptolemy's Geographia (2nd Century), which calls the region Kirrhadia after the Kirata population.[ 60n]
The first mention of the Kamarupa kingdom comes from the 4th Century Allahabad inscription of Samudragupta, which calls the kings of Kamarupa (western Assam) and Davaka (modern Nagaon district) frontier rulers (pratyanta nripati).[60o] The Chinese traveler Xuanzang visited the kingdom in the 7th Century, when it was ruled by Bhaskar Varman.[ 60p]
The corpus of Kamarupa inscriptions left by the rulers of Kamarupa, including Bhaskar Varman, at various places in Assam and present-day Bangladesh are important sources of information. Nevertheless, local grants completely eschew the name Kamarupa; instead they use the name Pragjyotisha, with the kings themselves called Pragjyotishadhipati.[ 60q]
According to the 10th Century Kalika Purana and the 7th Century Xuanzang, the western boundary was the historical Karatoya River. The eastern border was the temple of the goddess Tamreshvari (Pūrvāte Kāmarūpasya devī Dikkaravasini, given in Kalika Purana) near present-day Sadiya[60r] in the eastern most corner of Assam, which also agrees with Xuanzang.[ 60s] The people of Kamarupa were aware of Sichuan, which lay two months' journey away from its eastern borders.
The southern boundary was near the border between the Dhaka and Mymensingh districts in modern Bangladesh. Thus Kamarupa spanned the entire Brahmaputra valley and at various times included present-day Bhutan and parts of Bangladesh. This is supported by the various epigraphic records found scattered over these regions. The kingdom appears to have broken up entirely by the 13th Century into smaller kingdoms and from among them rose the Kamata kingdom in the west and the Ahom kingdom in the east, as the main successor kingdoms.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She cut a thick slice of bread and spread it with butter, then wrapped the rest in paper.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Partitive 'of' after the concrete quantifier head 'slice', with 'and' joining physical actions; the hypothesis puts both link and coordination in its 0-0.4 band.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: It took ten minutes for the bus to reach the depot at the end of the lane.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Temporal 'for' ('ten minutes for the bus', 0.2-0.3) and partitive 'of' after 'end', with no abstract head anywhere in the sentence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The roof of the old barn had leaked for years before anyone came to mend it.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Concrete 'of' head ('the roof'), temporal 'for years' and the named physical verb 'leaked', all listed as 0-0.4 cases.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The College of Engineering moved its offices into the north wing last autumn.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Proper-name head ('the College of', given in the hypothesis at 0.0) inside a concrete relocation narrative.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: He hammered the tiles onto the roof, wiped his hands on his trousers, and sat on the step.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Spatial 'on' twice, named physical verbs and concrete nouns, and an 'and' coordinating concrete actions rather than abstract words.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: They washed the soil off the rope, then laid the tiles out to dry in the sun.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Physical procedure built from the hypothesis's own inactive vocabulary (soil, rope, tiles, washed, laid), with no link or head.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Measure two cups of ice, pour them into the pan, and stir until the mixture thickens.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Recipe measurement: quantified partitive 'of' after 'cups', physical imperatives and no classificatory head.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The mill pond was still and green, and the old boat sat tied to the post.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Part-of-speech change: 'still' is the adjective here, not the connective of written argument the hypothesis claims at 0.5-1.2.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The men and children carried the nets down to the shore a while later.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Part-of-speech change: 'while' is a noun, and 'men and children' is exactly the human coordination the hypothesis puts at 0.0.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: We waited about ten minutes for the kettle to boil on the camp stove.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Part-of-speech change: 'about' is an approximating adverb, not a link governed by a head, while 'for' is temporal and 'on' spatial.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She left the light on and went upstairs to bed without a word.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Part-of-speech change: 'on' is a verb particle and 'and' joins concrete actions, so no claimed link or abstract head is present.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The children were quiet, for it was late and they had walked a long way.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Part-of-speech change: 'for' is a coordinating conjunction with no abstract head, the use the hypothesis excludes from its link class.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She changed her mind when the committee rejected the proposal on Friday.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Adverbial time clause with 'when', not a question or embedded question, and abstract nouns with no link or exposition verb beside them.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The children gasped at what a lovely little cottage they had built by the river.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Construction change: 'what' is an exclamative determiner, not an interrogative opening a question or embedded question.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Everyone was surprised how strange the old house looked in the fog.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Exclamative degree 'how' with no question or embedded question, so the hypothesis's interrogative class does not apply.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: From the ridge you can view the whole valley and the river below.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Part-of-speech change: 'view' is a physical verb, not the abstract head noun the hypothesis lists among its firing vocabulary.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The engineer explained what the pump does and how it draws water from the well beside the mill.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: It remains unclear, however, whether the two groups differ at all in their response to treatment.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The purpose of the survey was to measure public trust in local councils.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Link 'of' governed by an abstract head ('purpose') with an abstract complement, a head not used in the examples.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Several reasons for the failure were listed in the memo, and none of them involved the weather.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Quantifier 'several' plus the abstract head 'reasons for' in a reported memo, a novel context for the claimed link.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The report is short, although it compares three methods of storing grain and recommends the cheapest.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Running prose combining 'although', 'compares', 'methods of' and 'recommends', which the hypothesis predicts fires but the layout rival says falls away.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The committee recommends that the policy be reviewed annually; therefore the costs of compliance must be compared with the benefits.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Policy-register sentence with 'recommends', 'therefore' and the abstract link 'costs of compliance', a genre unlike the scan examples.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The morning was cold. Marta walked to the harbour, where the boats rocked, and wondered why the town had grown so quiet.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The embedded-question 'why' sits deep inside narration after 'wondered', which the hypothesis says fires from the text's second token onward.

adversarial_test_results.detail: Connective 'although' inside physical narration: the hypothesis's connective class fires, while the frame-only rival and the layout rival both predict quiet.

readings.explanation: Retrospective detector of the vocabulary of abstract construal - the words a written text uses to frame, ask about, classify and organize its subject rather than to name concrete things and physical events. It peaks (0.9-1.6) on (i) the interrogative words what, why and how (and less reliably whether, where, when, which) opening a question or an embedded question ('she explained how...' 1.20, 'we know what you mean' 1.0-1.3, 'it is uncertain whether...' 0.77); (ii) the links of, for, about and on when they carry the complement of an abstract head ('a common method of raising money' 1.56, 'several reasons for the delay' 1.54, 'types of soil' 1.0, 'tips for saving money' 0.94, 'the criteria for the award' 0.69, 'an overview of' 0.84) but only weakly (0-0.3) when the same links attach to a concrete, partitive, temporal or proper head ('a loaf of bread' 0.0, 'ten minutes for the bus' 0.2-0.3, 'for three hours' 0.0, 'the College of' 0.0); (iii) the verbs of describing, explaining, analysing and organizing (describe, explain, discuss, suggest, recommend, consider, examine, compare, present) at 0.6-1.5, with the abstract head nouns they take (aspect, method, reasons, criteria, overview, type, framework, view, information, research, quality) firing more weakly and unevenly on their own (0.2-0.95: overview and aspect strongest, method and results weakest) and clearly when a link or an exposition verb sits beside them; and (iv) the connectives and quantifiers of written argument (although, while, because, however, moreover, thus, therefore, still, even, only, such, both, each, several, most, all, another, indeed) at 0.5-1.2, and 'and'/'or' where it coordinates abstract words ('research and', 'quality and', 'cultural and' 0.6-0.9) but not concrete or human ones ('children and', 'men and' 0.0). It stays in the 0-0.4 band on narration and physical procedure - personal pronouns, the definite article, concrete nouns for objects, substances, places and people (roof, tiles, rope, bread, oven, soil, ice), physical verbs (leaked, carried, poured, hammered, washed, sat) and measurements - and because a text's first token is read with no context whatever, its first-position value is a bare-token prior (high on A/An, numerals, what/why/how/whether/when, although, this, about; near zero on he/she/they/my, the, in/at), so predictions of inactivity are for the text from its second token onward.

Narrower, frame-only reading: the pole detects complement frames rather than a register, so besides the interrogatives it should fire on of/for/about only where an abstract head actually governs a complement, and any abstract noun or exposition verb standing without a complement (the system, the process, describe it again) should stay inactive.

Broader, plain abstractness reading: the pole is a general abstract-versus-concrete register detector, so it should also fire on abstract nouns and nominalizations that take no complement (the conclusion, the problem, the process) and on any abstract word embedded in otherwise concrete narration.

Structural reading: the pole marks document layout rather than construal - headings, colons, newlines, list markers and section words (Overview, Steps, Results, Table of Contents, 'A.', Reference:) - so it should fire on section headings and list cues of any content and fall away in running body prose.
